4540:
Disgrace means the loss of other people's respect, approval, or good opinion — usually because of something shameful, wrong, or deeply disappointing that someone (or something) has done or represents.

Think of "grace" as being in a good standing with others — respected, approved of, thought well of. Disgrace is the opposite: you have fallen out of that good standing. People now look at you with shame, disappointment, or contempt instead of respect.
The Two Main Ways "Disgrace" Is Used as a Noun

1. Disgrace as a condition or state

This is when a person (or group) is in disgrace — meaning they are living in a state where others have lost respect for them. Their reputation has been damaged, and society, their community, or people close to them now look down on them or want nothing to do with them.

"The minister resigned and lived in disgrace for the rest of his life."

Here, "disgrace" refers to the ongoing state he is stuck in — a cloud of shame that hangs over him in the eyes of others.

"She returned home in disgrace after being caught cheating in the exam."

Notice that disgrace often involves a fall — the person was once in good standing, and now they are not. This fall from respect is central to the word.

2. Disgrace as a person or thing that causes shame

Here, "a disgrace" is used to describe someone or something that is so bad, wrong, or embarrassing that it brings shame — either to themselves, to others connected to them, or to a standard that is expected.

"You are a disgrace to this family."
"The condition of this hospital is an absolute disgrace."
"The referee's decision was a disgrace to the sport."

In these cases, the word isn't about a person falling from respect — it's about pointing at something and saying: this is so bad, so wrong, or so unacceptable that it is shameful. It embarrasses everyone around it or everyone associated with it.
What Makes Disgrace Different from Simply "Bad" or "Wrong"

Many things can be bad or wrong. But "disgrace" carries a specific extra weight: the element of shame and social judgment.

  • Something is bad if it causes harm or is incorrect.
  • Something is a disgrace if it is bad and it reflects shamefully on someone — it damages their image, their honor, or the image of something they represent.

For example:

  • A pothole on a road is "bad."
  • A road full of potholes that a city has ignored for years, while people pay taxes and suffer — that is "a disgrace." The word says: this is not just a problem; this is something that should embarrass the people responsible.

The word carries moral weight. It implies that something ought not to be this way, and that the people involved should feel ashamed.
The Public and Social Nature of Disgrace

Disgrace almost always involves other people's judgment. You can feel shame privately inside yourself, but disgrace is about how the outside world sees you.

This is important: a person is in disgrace not just because they feel bad about what they did, but because others — society, their community, their family, their institution — have withdrawn their respect and approval.

This is why disgrace is often connected to public figures. A politician, a celebrity, a sports star — they can fall into disgrace when something they did becomes publicly known and people turn against them. The disgrace is real partly because it is witnessed.
The Idea of Falling Into Disgrace

One of the most natural ways to use this noun is with the verb "fall" or "bring":

  • Fall into disgrace — to gradually or suddenly lose the respect and good opinion of others.
  • Bring disgrace (upon someone/something) — to cause others to lose respect for that person, family, or group through your actions.

"The captain brought disgrace upon the entire regiment."
"After the scandal, the once-celebrated scientist fell into disgrace."

Both phrases highlight that disgrace involves a change — from honor to shame, from respect to contempt.

Disgrace can range in intensity:

  • A mild disgrace might be something embarrassing that causes people to lose a bit of respect for you — like a professional making a careless, public mistake.
  • A deep disgrace is a serious, lasting loss of honor — a betrayal, a moral failure, a crime — that permanently changes how the world sees you.

Writers and speakers often intensify the word: "an utter disgrace," "an absolute disgrace," "a complete disgrace" — all of these signal that the shame involved is severe and total.
A Subtle but Important Shade: Disgrace Can Be Unfair

While disgrace often comes from genuinely bad actions, history is full of cases where people were disgraced unjustly — accused wrongly, punished for political reasons, or shamed for things that were not truly their fault. In those contexts, the word "disgrace" still accurately describes their condition (the world turned against them, their reputation was destroyed), even though the cause was unjust.

This shows that disgrace is about social reality — what people believe and how they treat you — not always about what is objectively true or fair.

Disgrace (noun) means:

  1. The state of having lost others' respect and approval, especially because of something shameful — being in disgrace.
  2. A person or thing that is so bad or wrong that it brings shame on itself or on others connected to it — being a disgrace.

The word always carries a sense of shame, damaged honor, and negative public judgment. It implies a standard was expected, it was broken, and now people are looking with contempt or disappointment. Whether it describes a fallen politician, a family member who behaved badly, or a crumbling public institution — "disgrace" tells you that something has failed not just in a practical way, but in a moral and social way that demands shame.
4541:
To disgruntle someone means to make them feel dissatisfied, displeased, and quietly resentful — especially because they feel they have been treated unfairly, let down, or ignored.

When you disgruntle someone, you don't terrify them or break their heart. You create a specific kind of unhappy feeling: a sulky, grumbling discontent. Think of someone who crosses their arms, sighs heavily, and mutters under their breath. That's what a disgruntled person looks like.

This is what makes the word special. The unhappiness it describes has a few specific ingredients:

  • A sense of grievance — the person feels wronged, overlooked, or short-changed.
  • Mild-to-moderate intensity — it's not explosive rage. It's the quiet, simmering kind of annoyance that stays with you.
  • A grumbling character — the person may complain, brood, or withdraw rather than shout or cry.

So if your boss gave you more work without extra pay, and you walked away feeling sour and resentful, your boss has disgruntled you.

People get disgruntled when:

  • They feel unfairly treated (a promotion they deserved went to someone else).
  • Their expectations were not met (a product they paid for didn't work well).
  • They feel ignored, undervalued, or dismissed.
  • Rules or decisions seem unreasonable or arbitrary to them.

FormExample
  • Base form: disgruntle — "Such policies disgruntle workers."
  • Third person present: disgruntles — "The new rule disgruntles everyone."
  • Past tense: disgruntled — "The decision disgruntled many customers."
  • Present participle: disgruntling — "The management's attitude was slowly disgruntling the whole team."

The important usage note: "disgruntled" is everywhere, "disgruntle" is rare

In everyday English, the verb disgruntle is almost never used directly. Instead, you'll almost always see its past participle used as an adjective:

"He was a disgruntled employee."
"The disgruntled customers demanded a refund."
"She left the meeting feeling disgruntled."

"Disgruntled" as an adjective simply means feeling dissatisfied, resentful, and sulkily unhappy. This is the form you'll encounter 95% of the time.

The straight verb form — "this disgruntles me" — is grammatically correct and proper, but it sounds slightly formal or literary. A native speaker would more naturally say "this makes me feel disgruntled" or "I'm disgruntled by this."

As a verb:

  • "The sudden policy change disgruntled the entire workforce."
  • "Cancelling the event at the last minute disgruntled many fans who had travelled far to attend."
  • "His dismissive reply disgruntled her, and she didn't speak to him for the rest of the day."

As the adjective "disgruntled" (for context):

  • "A disgruntled former employee filed a complaint."
  • "The disgruntled passengers waited three hours without any explanation."
  • "She sounded disgruntled on the phone."
How it differs from similar words

Understanding a word fully means knowing what makes it different from its neighbours.

  • Annoy — milder, more casual, often momentary. A mosquito annoys you. A buzzing sound annoys you. Disgruntling involves a deeper sense of unfairness or let-down.
  • Upset — broader and more emotionally intense. You can be upset about a death, a breakup, or a failure. Disgruntlement is specifically about dissatisfaction and grievance, not sadness or shock.
  • Anger/enrage — much stronger. These suggest hot, intense fury. To disgruntle is to create a cooler, more sullen discontent.
  • Disappoint — close, but disappointment focuses on unmet hope or expectation. Disgruntlement adds a layer of feeling wronged or hard done by.

If "disappoint" is when someone lets you down and you feel sad, disgruntle is when someone lets you down and you feel cheated.

"Disgruntle" and "disgruntled" are standard English — neither slang nor overly technical. They appear comfortably in news articles, formal writing, workplace communication, and everyday speech. They carry a slightly dry, understated tone, which makes them feel fitting when you want to describe someone's irritation without being too dramatic about it.

To disgruntle someone is to make them feel dissatisfied, resentful, and sulkily unhappy — especially by treating them in a way that feels unfair or dismissive. The past participle, disgruntled, used as an adjective, is by far the more common form you'll encounter in real life.
4542:
Disgruntled describes a person who feels a mix of anger, annoyance, and dissatisfaction — specifically because they feel they have been treated unfairly, let down, or ignored.

Think of it as three feelings happening at the same time:

  1. "I'm not happy with how things turned out." (dissatisfaction)
  2. "I feel like I was treated wrongly." (a sense of grievance)
  3. "Nobody seems to care about my concerns." (a feeling of being dismissed)

When all three of these feelings sit inside a person, that person is disgruntled.

Disgruntled is not the feeling of explosive, hot anger. It is more of a slow, simmering bitterness — the kind that sits in your chest and doesn't go away. It is the feeling of someone who has been silently suffering a complaint and feels nothing is being done about it.

Imagine an employee who has been working hard for three years, never received a promotion, and feels their manager doesn't appreciate them. They don't scream or quit on the spot. Instead, they walk around with a dark cloud over their head — muttering under their breath, doing the bare minimum, and feeling bitter about it all. That person is disgruntled.
Where It Is Most Commonly Used

The word is used very often in workplaces, organizations, and customer situations — any place where a person had an expectation and felt it wasn't met.

Common phrases you will hear:

  • "A disgruntled employee" — a worker who feels mistreated, underpaid, overlooked, or disrespected by their company.
  • "A disgruntled customer" — a buyer who feels cheated, ignored, or poorly served.
  • "A disgruntled voter" — a citizen who feels the government or a political party has failed or betrayed them.

These combinations are so common that "disgruntled employee" is practically a set phrase in English.

Here are examples that show the word working naturally in context:

  • "The disgruntled workers gathered outside the office to protest their low wages."
  • "After waiting two hours with no explanation, the customer left the store feeling disgruntled."
  • "He had been passed over for promotion twice, and his colleagues could tell he was growing increasingly disgruntled."
  • "The new manager had to deal with a team of disgruntled employees who had been neglected for years."

Notice that in every example, the person didn't just feel sad. They felt wronged, and that feeling shows in their attitude and behavior.
The Emotional Intensity — Where Does It Sit?

It helps to understand where disgruntled sits on the emotional scale:

Mild → Moderate → Strong → Intense

Slightly annoyed → Dissatisfied → Disgruntled → Resentful → Furious

Disgruntled sits in the moderate-to-strong zone. It is meaningfully stronger than simply being "a little annoyed" or "a bit disappointed." But it is not as intense as "furious" or "outraged." It carries a weight — a heaviness — that comes from the feeling of injustice left unaddressed over time.
How It Is Different From Similar Words

These words feel close to disgruntled, but they are not the same:

Dissatisfied — This is neutral and mild. You can be dissatisfied with a meal without feeling wronged. Disgruntled is stronger and always carries the sense of being treated unfairly.

Unhappy — A very general word. You can be unhappy for many reasons — grief, loss, loneliness. Disgruntled is specific: it's about feeling mistreated or let down by a person, system, or situation.

Resentful — Very close in meaning, but resentful focuses more on bitterness toward a specific person or past event. Disgruntled is more of a general state of bitter dissatisfaction, often about a situation rather than one person.

Discontented — This means generally unhappy with one's circumstances. Disgruntled adds the extra layer of anger and the sense of being specifically wronged.

Disgruntled almost always implies that the person once had reasonable expectations — they weren't asking for too much. They expected fair treatment, fair pay, a basic level of respect, or a promise to be kept. When those expectations were not met, and especially when they felt their concerns were brushed aside or ignored, they became disgruntled.

This is why the word carries moral weight. When you call someone disgruntled, you are not dismissing them as simply moody or difficult. You are acknowledging that their dissatisfaction likely has a real cause.

Disgruntled means feeling angry, bitter, and dissatisfied — especially because you feel you were treated unfairly or that your concerns were ignored. It is a slow, simmering kind of resentment, not explosive rage. It is most often used to describe workers, customers, or members of a group who feel let down by those in power.
4543:
A disguise is anything used to change or hide someone's true appearance, identity, or nature — so that others cannot recognize or identify them correctly.

The key idea behind a disguise is deliberate deception: you are not just changing how you look, you are specifically trying to make others believe you are someone (or something) you are not.
What a disguise can consist of

A disguise is often a combination of physical changes:

  • Wearable items: a wig, a hat, a mask, different clothing, glasses, a fake beard or mustache
  • Cosmetic changes: heavy makeup, face paint, prosthetic features, colored contact lenses
  • Behavioral changes: a fake accent, an altered voice, a different way of walking or carrying yourself

A disguise that uses only one of these might be easy to see through. The more layers it has, the more convincing it becomes.

A disguise is always built around a goal — to prevent recognition. This is what makes it different from simply wearing a costume or dressing up for fun.

When a child puts on a superhero costume at a party, everyone still knows who the child is. No one is being deceived. That is a costume, not a disguise.

But when a spy changes their appearance so that enemies will not recognize them, every element of that changed appearance — the different clothes, the altered voice, the fake name — forms a disguise, because the clear intent is to deceive.

This is the defining quality of a disguise: the intent to make others see something false.

Because a disguise is meant to hide the truth, we often talk about seeing through a disguise — meaning someone was clever or observant enough to realize that what they were seeing was not real. If a prince disguises himself as a merchant in the marketplace, and a sharp-eyed guard notices his royal ring, that guard has seen through the disguise.

A convincing disguise is one where no one suspects anything — the false identity is accepted completely.
A thin disguise is one that barely conceals the truth — almost anyone paying attention can tell it is fake.

"Disguise" is also widely used in an abstract, figurative sense — not for physical appearance, but for anything that hides its true nature.

  • "His warm politeness was a disguise for his deep resentment."
    Here, the politeness is called a disguise because it hides a real feeling underneath.
  • "The new tax was just an old idea in disguise."
    The idea looks new and different, but underneath, it is the same old thing.

In this figurative sense, a disguise is a surface layer that presents a false picture of what truly lies beneath — whether that "thing" is a motive, a feeling, an idea, or an agenda.

As a noun, "disguise" works in two ways:

Countable — when you refer to a specific, physical disguise:

  • "He wore a disguise."
  • "She had three different disguises prepared."

Uncountable — when you refer to the general state or concept of being disguised:

  • "The spy arrived in disguise." (No article; it means "in a state of concealment.")
  • "She was a master of disguise."

"In disguise"
Simply means wearing or using a disguise — being outwardly different from who you truly are.
"The detective walked through the neighborhood in disguise, listening to conversations."

"A blessing in disguise"
This is one of the most widely used expressions in English. It means something that looks bad or unfortunate at first, but turns out to be good in the end. The "blessing" (the good thing) is hidden inside the appearance of misfortune — wearing misfortune as its disguise.
"Failing that exam was a blessing in disguise — it made me study harder and truly understand the subject."

"Master of disguise"
Someone who is exceptionally skilled at changing their identity or appearance — someone who can fool almost anyone.
"The fictional spy was a master of disguise, capable of becoming a completely different person within minutes."

"Under the disguise of" (also: under the guise of)
Means pretending to be or do one thing while actually being or doing something else.
"Under the disguise of a business trip, he was actually investigating his competitors."

"Without disguise"
Means openly, honestly, without hiding anything.
"She stated her disappointment without disguise — her face and words made her feelings completely clear."

A disguise (noun) is:

Anything — physical, behavioral, or abstract — that conceals the true identity or nature of a person or thing, with the specific purpose of making others believe something false.

It is the tool of anyone — a spy, a fugitive, an actor, or even a manipulative idea — that needs to appear as something it is not.
4544:
To disguise something means to change its appearance, nature, or character so that others will not recognize it for what it truly is.

The most important thing to understand is this: disguising is not the same as hiding. When you hide something, you remove it from sight — it's gone. When you disguise something, it is still there, still visible, still present — but it has been made to look or seem like something else entirely.

The truth exists. But it is wearing a false face.
A Mental Image to Anchor the Word

Imagine a wolf that puts on a sheep's fleece and walks into a flock of sheep. The wolf has not disappeared. It is right there among the sheep. But everything the other sheep can see tells them: "this is one of us." The wolf has disguised itself.

This is the heart of the word: something real is hidden behind a false appearance that is itself visible and believable.
The Three Things That Always Happen When You Disguise

Whenever the word "disguise" is used correctly, these three things are at play:

  1. A true identity, nature, or quality exists.
  2. That truth is deliberately concealed.
  3. A false appearance is put in its place, so others perceive something different from the reality.

The goal is always some form of deception — whether harmless (a costume at a party), protective (a spy avoiding capture), or dishonest (a fraudster hiding real intentions).

1. Disguising a person's physical appearance

This is the most familiar use. You change how someone looks so that others don't recognize them.

  • "The spy disguised herself as a local shopkeeper."
  • "He disguised himself with a false beard, a wig, and tinted glasses."

Notice the common pattern: disguise oneself as [someone or something]. The person is not gone — they are right there — but their true identity is buried under a false one.

You can also disguise another person, not just yourself:

  • "The witness protection programme disguised him as a retired schoolteacher."

2. Disguising feelings and emotions

Feelings are invisible, but they show up on your face, in your voice, and in your body language. When you disguise an emotion, you don't just suppress it (push it inward so nothing shows) — you go further: you actively replace it by showing something different.

  • "She disguised her nervousness by speaking slowly and confidently."
  • "He couldn't disguise his jealousy, even though he was smiling."
  • "She disguised her deep sadness behind loud, constant laughter."

In the first example, the nervousness is the truth; the slow, confident speaking is the false appearance put in its place. The nervousness is still there — it's just hidden behind its opposite.

3. Disguising intentions and motives

People often hide their real purpose — what they actually want or plan to do — by presenting an innocent, acceptable-looking purpose instead.

  • "The corrupt minister disguised his theft of public funds as 'development expenditure.'"
  • "She disguised her visit to his house as a casual neighbourly check-in, when in truth she wanted to find out if he had read her letter."

The real intention is hidden; a harmless or respectable one is shown in its place.

4. Disguising something abstract — making a negative thing appear as something else

"Disguise" is also used when something unpleasant, bad, or dishonest is dressed up to look different from what it really is.

  • "Don't disguise your fear of hard work as 'waiting for the right moment.'"
  • "The company disguised its massive price hike as a 'minor adjustment for inflation.'"
  • "His cruelty was disguised as blunt honesty — he claimed he was just 'telling the truth.'"

In each case, a real quality (fear, a price hike, cruelty) is hidden behind a false, more flattering label.

5. Disguising a physical quality — taste, smell, or texture

In everyday practical life, you can disguise a bad sensory quality by overwhelming it with something else, so that the senses are misled into not fully registering the original.

  • "The strong spices in the dish disguised the slightly stale meat."
  • "She used a heavy perfume to disguise the smell of smoke on her clothes."

The bad quality is technically still present — but what reaches the senses is the false cover placed over it.
How "Disguise" Differs from Words That Look Similar

Disguise vs. Hide
When you hide something, it disappears from view — it's not accessible to others. When you disguise something, it remains visible and present, but looks like something it is not. A person hiding in a closet is out of sight. A person in disguise is standing right in front of you, appearing to be someone else.

Disguise vs. Conceal
To conceal means to keep something from being seen or known — it is a deliberate form of hiding. Disguise goes one step further: instead of just preventing something from being seen, you replace it with a false version. You can conceal your discomfort by staying silent and expressionless; you disguise it by actively behaving as if you are comfortable and relaxed.

Disguise vs. Mask
To mask something means to cover it — like putting something over it. The word suggests a surface-level cover, like a lid placed on something. "Disguise" implies a deeper, more thorough transformation: the thing doesn't just have a cover on it; it genuinely appears to be something different.

Disguise vs. Pretend
To pretend is to claim or act as if something is true when it is not — it is about your own behaviour and assertions. To disguise is about shaping what others actually perceive, by creating a false appearance in the real world. You pretend to be happy in what you say and do; you disguise your unhappiness by creating a convincing physical appearance of happiness.
The Essential Qualities of the Word

It is always intentional. You choose to disguise. It does not happen by accident. Nothing disguises itself without a deliberate act.

It involves replacement, not removal. The truth is not taken away. It stays there, underneath. A false appearance is placed over it. This is what makes disguising so different from simply hiding: the original thing is still present.

It aims to mislead. The purpose is always to make others (or sometimes yourself) believe something is different from what it truly is.
Degree: How Well Can Something Be Disguised?

Disguising is not always fully successful. You can disguise something completely, partially, or barely at all:

  • Completely: "She disguised her accent so perfectly that no one suspected she was foreign."
  • Poorly / barely: "He barely disguised his contempt for his colleagues." (It was obvious, despite the attempt.)
  • With difficulty: "She struggled to disguise her excitement."

When someone "couldn't disguise" a feeling or quality, it means the truth showed through despite the attempt to cover it.

PatternExample
disguise oneself as [someone]"He disguised himself as a security guard."
disguise something as [something else]"She disguised the insult as a compliment."
disguise one's voiceto alter how one sounds to avoid recognition
barely / hardly disguise"He barely disguised his boredom."
in disguise (related noun phrase)"a blessing in disguise" — something that seems bad but turns out to be good; its true, positive nature was hidden

To disguise is to deliberately give something a false appearance — not by making it disappear, but by making it look, sound, or seem like something it is not, so that its true nature goes unrecognized.
4545:
Disgust is a strong, deeply unpleasant feeling of revulsion — a powerful inner reaction that says "this is wrong, offensive, or foul, and I want nothing to do with it."

It is not simply disliking something. It is much more intense than that. When you feel disgust, something inside you recoils. You want to turn away, pull back, or get as far away as possible from whatever is causing the feeling.

Disgust works on two levels, and understanding both is key.

1. Physical disgust
This is the kind felt in your body. Your stomach churns, your face scrunches up, you feel nauseous, and you instinctively want to look away or leave. It is triggered by things that feel contaminating, rotten, or unclean — spoiled food, foul smells, filth, bodily waste, maggots, or the sight of something decaying.

This kind of disgust is almost automatic. You do not have to think about it — your body reacts before your mind does.

2. Moral disgust
This is the kind directed at people's behavior, actions, or character. When someone is cruel, dishonest, corrupt, or deeply unfair, you can feel a strong moral revulsion toward what they did or who they are. Your body may not feel sick, but emotionally, you feel the same pulling-away — a deep sense of "this is unacceptable."

Example: Watching a powerful person exploit the vulnerable can fill someone with disgust even if no rotten smell is involved.
What makes disgust different from other emotions

This is where many learners get confused, so let's be precise.

Disgust vs. Dislike
Dislike is mild and ordinary. You can dislike a song, a flavor, or a person's habit without being disgusted. Disgust is far more intense — it involves revulsion, not just preference.

Disgust vs. Anger
Anger wants to confront or fight back. Disgust wants to withdraw. When you are angry, you move toward something; when you are disgusted, you pull away from it.

Disgust vs. Contempt
Contempt is about feeling superior — looking down on someone. Disgust is about revulsion — feeling repelled by someone or something. You can feel contempt without revulsion. You can feel disgust without thinking yourself superior.

Disgust vs. Hatred
Hatred includes a wish for harm, a long-burning hostility. Disgust is specifically about the repulsion and the desire to distance. Hatred can last quietly in the background; disgust tends to be triggered by a specific sight, act, or encounter.

Disgust vs. Distaste
Distaste is the polite, controlled, mild cousin of disgust. If you say "I find that in poor taste," that is distaste. If you say "I feel sick looking at that," that is disgust.
The core quality of disgust: contamination

One of the most distinctive features of disgust is the sense of contamination — the feeling that contact with the disgusting thing has somehow "dirtied" or "tainted" you. Even thinking about it too long can make you feel contaminated.

This is why people say things like "I feel dirty just hearing that" or "I need to wash my hands after touching that." The disgust is not just about the thing itself — it is about the sense that it reaches you and leaves a mark.

Disgust sits at the stronger end of the emotional spectrum. It ranges from mild to overwhelming:

  • A mild version: You see something slightly unclean and feel a flicker of discomfort — a faint sense of "ugh."
  • A moderate version: You smell something rotten and your face twists, your stomach turns, and you step away quickly.
  • A strong version: You witness a deeply cruel act and feel a wave of moral revulsion so powerful it is almost physical — a feeling of outrage mixed with sickness.
Common synonyms and how they differ

• Revulsion — nearly identical to disgust, but leans slightly more toward the physical and bodily reaction.
  • Repulsion — emphasizes the push-away quality; being "repelled" by something as if by a force.
  • Loathing — stronger and more personal; closer to intense hatred mixed with disgust.
  • Repugnance — formal word; used especially for moral disgust at something deeply offensive.
  • Abhorrence — very formal; the strongest of these synonyms; implies profound moral rejection.
  • Aversion — milder; more like a strong, persistent tendency to avoid something rather than a sharp emotional reaction.
How disgust is used in sentences

Pay attention to these natural patterns:

  • "filled with disgust" — She was filled with disgust when she saw how the animals were treated.
  • "a look / expression of disgust" — He gave a look of disgust and pushed the plate away.
  • "in disgust" — She walked out in disgust after hearing the speech.
  • "to someone's disgust" — To her disgust, the report had been buried by the committee.
  • "with disgust" — He stared at the mess with disgust.
  • "feel / show / hide disgust" — She tried hard to hide her disgust, but her face gave her away.
  • "utter disgust / sheer disgust" — The public reacted with utter disgust at the cover-up.
  • "a sense of disgust" — A sense of disgust washed over him as he read the letter.
A few real-world examples to cement it

The journalist's investigation revealed corruption so deep it filled the entire country with disgust.

Here, disgust is moral — directed at the wrongdoing.

She opened the fridge, and the smell that hit her made her step back in disgust.

Here, disgust is physical — triggered by something rotten.

He sat through the meeting in silence, barely managing to conceal his disgust at the way his colleague was treated.

Here, disgust is again moral — a reaction to witnessing something unjust or cruel.

Disgust is a powerful, deeply unpleasant feeling of revulsion — physical, moral, or both — that makes you want to pull away from whatever has violated your sense of what is clean, acceptable, or right.
4546:
A dish is a container — usually round, flat or slightly hollow — used to hold, cook, or serve food. Think of the round plate your meal is served on, or the deeper bowl-like container your mother might put a roast chicken in before placing it on the dinner table. That object is a dish.

The key physical features of a dish are:

  • It is wider than it is deep (unlike a cup or a jar, which are tall).
  • It has low or no walls, or sometimes gently raised edges, so you can easily reach the food inside.
  • It is meant to hold things — especially food — and present them.

A dish sits somewhere between a plate (very flat, minimal edges) and a bowl (deeper, more rounded). In everyday use, "dish" is a broader, more flexible word that can refer to either.

"She placed the salad in a large dish and set it in the middle of the table."

This is the most literal meaning — the physical object itself.

Dishes can be made of ceramic, porcelain, glass, metal, or even wood. They come in many sizes and shapes — round, oval, square — but they all share the purpose of holding food for cooking or serving.

"He put the pasta in a serving dish."
"The oven dish was still hot when she took it out."

Note the slight difference in use:

  • A serving dish is what you bring to the table for everyone to take food from.
  • A baking dish or oven dish is what you cook food inside in the oven.
  • A side dish (which leads us to Meaning 2) is a smaller, separate portion of food served alongside the main meal.
Meaning 2: A Type or Preparation of Food

This is the meaning you'll encounter most often in everyday conversation, and it's important to understand it clearly.

Here, "dish" does not refer to the container. It refers to a specific type of food, or a specific way food is prepared and served. The word shifts from meaning the object to meaning the food itself.

"Paella is a traditional Spanish dish."
"What is your favorite dish?"
"The chef prepared three dishes for the dinner."

In these sentences, nobody is talking about a plate or a bowl. They are talking about a complete food item — a recipe, a meal, or a preparation.

Think of it this way: when a chef creates a new recipe — say, grilled salmon with lemon butter — that entire creation is called a dish. It has a name, ingredients, and a method of cooking. It is one dish.

A dish in this sense can be:

  • A main dish — the central, most important food of a meal (e.g., roast chicken, steak, curry).
  • A side dish — a smaller food served alongside the main dish to complement it (e.g., mashed potatoes, steamed vegetables, bread).
  • A starter dish / appetizer — food served at the beginning of a meal before the main course.

"Rice is a staple dish in many Asian countries."
"The restaurant's signature dish is their lamb stew."

Why does the word "dish" get used this way?
Because food was historically placed in a dish (the container) before being served. Over time, people began using the word to refer to the food itself, not just the container holding it. This shift is very natural in language.
Meaning 3: "The Dishes" — All the Tableware Used for a Meal

When "dish" is used in the plural form — "the dishes" — it refers collectively to all the plates, bowls, cups, glasses, and utensils that have been used during a meal and now need to be washed.

"Can you wash the dishes after dinner?"
"She spent twenty minutes doing the dishes."

This is a very common household phrase. "Doing the dishes" or "washing the dishes" means cleaning up all the tableware after eating. Notice that it doesn't just mean literal dishes — it means everything used: cups, spoons, pots, pans, etc. "Dishes" here is used as a general word for the whole collection of things to be cleaned.

A satellite dish is a large, bowl-shaped device — typically mounted on a rooftop or wall — used to receive television or radio signals from satellites orbiting the Earth.

"They installed a satellite dish on the roof to get better TV channels."

The reason this device is called a "dish" is simple and visual: it looks like a dish — it is wide, round, and curved inward (concave), just like a large bowl or dish. The shape is functional: the curved surface collects and focuses signals toward a central receiver point.

In everyday speech, people often just say "dish" instead of "satellite dish":

"The dish on their house can pick up hundreds of channels."

In informal, conversational English — especially in American English — "dish" (or more commonly "the dish") can mean gossip, rumor, or exciting private information about someone or something.

"Come on, give me the dish — what happened at the party?"
"She always has the latest dish on everyone in the office."

Here, "dish" is used the same way you might use words like "gossip," "news," "scoop," or "tea" (in modern slang). It suggests information that is juicy, private, and entertaining.

This meaning is informal and mostly spoken. You wouldn't typically see it in formal writing.
Meaning 6 (Informal, Somewhat Dated): An Attractive Person

In informal English — more common in older British usage but still understood today — calling someone "a dish" means they are very attractive or good-looking.

"Did you see the new colleague? He's quite a dish!"
"She walked in and everyone noticed — a real dish."

This usage is lighthearted and complimentary, though it is considered a bit old-fashioned today. You're more likely to hear it from older speakers or in older films and books, but it still appears in modern casual speech sometimes.
Meaning 7: Any Bowl-Shaped or Concave Object

Beyond food and satellites, "dish" can refer to any object or surface that has a concave, bowl-like shape — something that curves inward like the inside of a bowl.

"The engineers designed a dish-shaped reflector for the telescope."
"The valley formed a natural dish in the landscape."

This meaning is used in technical, scientific, and descriptive contexts. Whenever something is shaped like the inside of a bowl — wide and curving inward — it can be called a dish or described as dish-shaped.

#MeaningExample
1A physical container for food"Put the chicken in the baking dish."
2A type or preparation of food"Sushi is a Japanese dish."
3"The dishes" = all tableware to clean"I'll do the dishes after dinner."
4A satellite dish (signal receiver)"The dish is mounted on the roof."
5Gossip or inside information (informal)"What's the dish on those two?"
6An attractive person (informal, older)"He's a real dish."
7Any bowl-shaped/concave object"A dish-shaped antenna."

Notice that almost every meaning of "dish" connects back to one central image: a wide, round, hollow, concave shape. A food dish is concave. A satellite dish is concave. An attractive person is described using the word because it evokes something appealing and well-presented (like a beautifully served dish of food). Gossip is called "dish" because it's something you "serve up" to others.

Once you hold that central image in your mind — something wide, open, curved, and used to hold or present something — the word "dish" becomes easy to understand across all its uses.

Imagine you've just woken up on a lazy Sunday morning. You're wandering around the house in your pajamas, or perhaps a loose robe that isn't properly tied. Your hair is undone. You haven't "put yourself together" yet. You're not naked — but you're certainly not dressed for the world.

That state — that in-between condition of being incompletely, loosely, or carelessly dressed — is dishabille.

It refers to the condition of being only partially dressed, or dressed in the informal, private garments one wears away from public view: nightgowns, underclothes, a loosely worn dressing gown, or clothing that is disheveled and not properly arranged.
What It Is — and What It Isn't

Dishabille is not nudity. That distinction matters. The word describes a specific zone between being fully dressed and being undressed. A person in dishabille is wearing something — but what they're wearing signals that they haven't prepared themselves to be seen by the outside world.

Think of it as the clothing of the private self: the clothes you'd be embarrassed to answer the front door in, or the state you'd be caught in if someone arrived unexpectedly early.

Some examples of what dishabille looks like in practice:

  • A person in a loosely draped robe, not properly fastened
  • Someone still in their nightclothes well into the morning
  • A person whose clothing is half-removed, carelessly hanging off them
  • Someone in undergarments, not yet or only partially dressed

The key ingredients are incompleteness and informality. Either the dressing process hasn't been finished, or the clothing itself is of the kind that belongs only in private.

The word has a particular weight to it. When writers use it, they're not merely reporting that someone is underdressed. They're pointing at something more layered.

Intimacy. Historically, and even today in literature, being seen in dishabille by someone was a sign of closeness and trust. You don't wander around in your nightclothes in front of strangers. Being in dishabille in someone's presence implied that you allowed them into your private world — or that you were caught off-guard and exposed in a vulnerable way.

Vulnerability and informality. There is something unguarded about dishabille. The person has not yet constructed their public self. They haven't put on their armour for the day. This gives the word a soft, sometimes intimate, sometimes slightly embarrassing quality.

A touch of elegance, even in undress. Because the word comes to English through French aristocratic culture, it has a certain refined quality even when describing something unglamorous. You'll notice it often appears in literary, historical, or formal writing — it isn't slang. Saying someone was "in dishabille" feels more graceful than saying they were "half-dressed."

As a noun, dishabille appears in a few natural constructions:

"In dishabille" — the most common phrasing. It means in a state of dishabille.

She answered the door in dishabille, clearly having been woken by the knock.

"A state of dishabille" — a slightly more formal way of saying the same thing.

The ambassador found his host in a state of dishabille, still wearing his dressing gown at noon.

Sometimes, "dishabille" is used to refer to the actual garment worn in that state — a loose, informal robe or negligee itself. In this use, the word names the item of clothing rather than the condition.

She wore a silk dishabille, soft and shapeless, clearly meant only for private hours.

This second use is less common today, but you may encounter it in older literature.

Because dishabille so strongly suggests being unprepared and unpolished, writers sometimes use it figuratively — beyond clothing — to describe a general state of disorder or unreadiness.

The manuscript was in dishabille: half-finished chapters, notes scattered through the margins, ideas that had never been properly dressed for the page.

Here, nothing is literally clothing. But the metaphor works precisely because dishabille already means "not yet put together properly." In figurative use, it means caught in a raw, unfinished, or exposed state.
How It Differs from Simpler Words

You might wonder: why not just say "undressed" or "half-dressed"? The distinction is real.

  • "Undressed" and "half-dressed" are neutral and clinical. They simply describe a degree of clothing.
  • Dishabille carries connotations of intimacy, informality, and the private sphere that those plainer words don't. It implies not just less clothing, but the specific context of private, domestic, unguarded existence.
  • It also often implies a certain carelessness — not merely that the dressing is incomplete, but that the person is in a state of casual disregard for their own appearance, as one naturally is in private.

If a character in a novel is described as "undressed," you picture simple incompleteness. If they are described as being "in dishabille," you picture something more evocative — a person at ease in their private world, vulnerable, not yet armored for public life.

Dishabille is the state of being incompletely, loosely, or carelessly dressed in private, informal garments — not naked, but not ready to face the world — carrying connotations of intimacy, vulnerability, and the unguarded private self.

To understand disharmony, you first need to picture what harmony means.

Harmony is a state where different elements — people, sounds, ideas, forces — fit together smoothly and peacefully. Think of a choir where every voice blends perfectly, or a team where every member works together without friction. That's harmony: different parts coexisting in a balanced, pleasing, conflict-free way.

Disharmony is the exact opposite. It is the state where things that should fit together — or are expected to work together — instead clash, conflict, or fail to coexist peacefully. It is the breakdown of that balance.

If harmony is a smooth, calm river flowing in one direction, disharmony is what happens when the water starts moving in conflicting directions, creating turbulence. The different currents don't cooperate — they fight each other.
Disharmony describes a condition of conflict, tension, or incompatibility between things that belong together. That "condition" can exist in many different areas of life.

1. Between people (the most common use)

This is where you'll see the word most often. When people in a group — a family, a team, a community, a nation — have ongoing disagreements, tensions, or conflicts that disturb the peace between them, there is disharmony.

There was growing disharmony within the company after the new policy was announced.

Years of disharmony between the two neighbors finally led to a legal dispute.

Notice that it's not just one argument — disharmony implies a state that persists, a tension that hangs in the air and affects how things function. It describes the general atmosphere of conflict, not just a single moment of disagreement.

2. In music

In music, harmony is when notes sound pleasing together — they blend. Disharmony (sometimes called discord) is when musical notes or sounds clash in a way that feels jarring, unpleasant, or unresolved to the ear. The notes don't blend; they fight each other.

The two instruments played in disharmony, making the audience uneasy.

3. Within a person (inner disharmony)

A person can experience disharmony within themselves. This happens when their thoughts, values, feelings, or desires are in conflict with each other — when different parts of their own inner world don't fit together.

She felt a deep disharmony between what she believed was right and what she was being asked to do.

4. Between abstract things — ideas, systems, elements

Disharmony can also describe a clash between concepts, forces, or elements in any system.

There is a clear disharmony between the government's promises and its actual actions.

The loud, modern building stood in disharmony with the quiet, ancient neighborhood around it.

In that last example, the building and the neighborhood clash — they don't fit together aesthetically or atmospherically. That mismatch is disharmony.

Understanding these qualities will help you use and recognize the word precisely:

It describes a state, not just an event.
Disharmony is not a single fight or clash. It is a condition — an ongoing state of things being out of alignment. When you say "there is disharmony," you mean the conflict or tension is present in the environment, not just that something went wrong once.

It implies something that should fit together, but doesn't.
The word carries an implicit expectation. We speak of disharmony between things that are supposed to be compatible or unified — family members, colleagues, musical notes, or a country's leaders. If two completely unrelated things don't match, we wouldn't call it disharmony. The word highlights a failure of something that was expected to work.

It can range from mild to severe.
Disharmony doesn't always mean outright war or chaos. It can be:

  • A quiet, underlying tension between coworkers
  • A noticeable but controlled disagreement between nations
  • A deep, destructive conflict within a community

The word covers the whole spectrum, from subtle unease to open strife.

It affects the whole, not just the parts.
When disharmony exists in a group or system, it doesn't just affect the two clashing elements — it affects the entire environment. A family in disharmony doesn't just have two unhappy members; the whole household feels the tension. This is what makes disharmony significant.

It's worth being clear about this, because learners sometimes overuse the word.

  • Simple difference is not disharmony. Two people can have completely different personalities, tastes, or opinions and still live or work together in complete peace. That's not disharmony — that's just difference. Disharmony requires friction or conflict arising from that difference.
  • A single argument is not disharmony. If two friends argue once and then make up, that wasn't disharmony — it was a disagreement. Disharmony refers to a sustained state of tension or conflict.
  • Change or imperfection is not disharmony. A team going through a difficult project isn't necessarily in disharmony. The word specifically points to a breakdown in cohesion or peace, not just stress or challenge.

Disharmony is a somewhat formal and serious word. When a writer or speaker uses it, they're signalling that the conflict or clash being described is significant — it's not trivial. It suggests that something that was (or should be) whole and balanced has been disrupted in a meaningful way.

It also carries a slightly abstract quality, which makes it useful for describing not just loud, visible conflicts but also quiet, underlying tensions that you can sense even if no one is shouting.

Knowing related words helps clarify a word's exact meaning:

  • Discord — very close in meaning; often used for disharmony between people or in music. Slightly stronger feeling of active conflict.
  • Friction — a milder, ongoing tension between people or ideas; like the early stages of disharmony.
  • Conflict — a broader word for any active struggle or disagreement; disharmony is more atmospheric and states how the environment feels, while conflict describes the struggle itself.
  • Strife — bitter, prolonged conflict; more intense than disharmony.
  • Division — when a group is split into opposing sides; can be a cause or symptom of disharmony.

The antonym (opposite) of disharmony is harmony — and also: accord, unity, peace, cohesion, concord.
One Final Way to Remember It

Imagine a beautiful painting where all the colors complement each other — that's harmony. Now imagine someone added a color that clashes horribly with everything else, making the whole painting feel wrong and uncomfortable. The painting is now in a state of disharmony.

The key: elements that should work together, don't — and the whole suffers for it.

That is disharmony.

To dishearten someone means to cause them to lose their courage, hope, confidence, or enthusiasm — to make them feel like giving up or feel that there is no point in continuing.

Think of it this way: your "heart," in an emotional sense, is the source of your drive, your hope, and your will to keep going. When something disheartens you, it strikes at that source and weakens it. You feel deflated, low in spirit, and less motivated than you were before.
The Key Idea to Always Remember

Dishearten is not simply about feeling sad. It is specifically about losing the inner fire to continue. It means something has knocked the spirit out of you.

A very important part of this word's meaning is that it implies you had hope, confidence, or motivation before — and now, because of something that happened, you have lost it (or at least a part of it). There is always a before and an after.

Before: You were hopeful, enthusiastic, or determined.
Something happens.
After: You feel low, discouraged, and less willing to push forward.

That gap — that loss — is exactly what "dishearten" describes.

Imagine you have been practising hard for a singing competition for months. You truly believe in yourself. Then, on the day of the competition, the judge dismisses your performance rudely without even listening properly.

That moment disheartens you. Your confidence dips. You start to wonder, "Is it even worth trying again?" Your spirit takes a blow.

That feeling — that sudden loss of heart — is what being disheartened feels like.
How It Is Used in Sentences

The word can be used in several natural ways:

Active form (something disheartens someone):

  • "The repeated failures disheartened him."
  • "Constant criticism can dishearten even the most motivated person."
  • "Losing the match so badly disheartened the young team."

Passive form (someone is disheartened by something):

  • "She was disheartened by the lack of support from her friends."
  • "He felt deeply disheartened after hearing the news."
  • "The volunteers were disheartened when their efforts seemed to go unnoticed."

As an adjective (disheartened):

  • "A disheartened student sat quietly in the corner."
  • "She looked disheartened after the meeting."

As another adjective (disheartening):

  • "It was a truly disheartening experience."
  • "The statistics are disheartening for young job seekers."

Dishearten sits in the middle of the emotional scale — it is stronger than simply feeling "a little disappointed," but it is not as total or permanent as being completely broken or destroyed in spirit. A disheartened person has taken a blow to their motivation or hope, but the implication is that they can recover — they are not necessarily finished.

This is why you often hear phrases like:

  • "Don't be disheartened." (meaning: don't let this knock you down permanently)
  • "Try not to feel disheartened." (there is still hope)

The word naturally carries with it the quiet suggestion that recovery is possible, which is part of what makes it different from stronger words like crush or devastate.
How Dishearten Differs from Similar Words

Discourage is the closest synonym and is almost always interchangeable with dishearten. However, discourage tends to feel slightly more practical — it often refers to being put off from doing a specific thing. Dishearten tends to feel slightly more emotional and deeper — it touches your overall spirit and sense of hope, not just a single action.

  • "The long queue discouraged me from going in." ✅ (practical, specific action)
  • "The long queue disheartened me." ✅ (but here it feels more emotional, like your whole mood dropped)

Demoralize is stronger and is more often used for groups (like an army, a team, or a workforce). It suggests a more serious collapse of morale. Dishearten can be used for both individuals and groups and feels more personal.

Dispirit is almost identical in meaning to dishearten and can be used in its place in nearly every situation. It is simply a little less common in everyday speech.

Dishearten is a slightly formal word, but it is completely natural in everyday conversation, writing, journalism, and literature. It is not stuffy or old-fashioned — you will hear it in news reports, books, office conversations, and daily speech without it sounding out of place.
All the Word Forms at a Glance

Since this is a verb, it changes form depending on how you use it:

  • dishearten — the base form ("Hard rejections dishearten writers.")
  • disheartens — third person singular, present tense ("Failure disheartens him easily.")
  • disheartened — past tense, or used as an adjective ("She disheartened the whole group." / "He looked disheartened.")
  • disheartening — present participle, or used as an adjective ("The results are disheartening.")
  • dishearteningly — the adverb form ("The turnout was dishearteningly low.")
To dishearten means to cause someone to lose their courage, hope, or enthusiasm — to drain the spirit out of them, making them feel like continuing is harder or less worthwhile than it seemed before.
